Great game to chill out and explore/fight/craft to awesome lofi-vibes music. Devs listen to feedback and push bugfixes and QOL frequently, while still not neglecting new features. They have their priorities right. If you want a cool survival game to get happily sucked into, give this a try. Good for casual players, hardcore players, and completionists. 

I would recommend using only cosmetic mods for a while (read: Early Access), though plenty other cool ideas exist in the Steam Workshop. The Fantasy Customizations mod never seems to break, no matter how many updates go by, and adds a lot of personality to your character. Most other mods seem to get a bit left behind, as the game changes significantly (mostly behind the scenes) with every update. Once Wayward settles down on major changes the modding community can take off, though. I look forward to seeing where this game goes! 

Major props to the soundtrack- I get instant serotonin upon loading up the game and hearing the music start. It's also dynamic (can be changed in settings if you don't like this) so it changes based on your situation, which is a nice indicator for me since I have bad vision and might miss something otherwise. Honestly, the audio feedback in general is helpful and great for accessibility.

The game is customizable to be as menu-lite or menu-heavy as you want. Set everything automatic in your toolbar and just walk into trees to chop them, or go through a menu to choose which action to take. It can be overwhelming at first, but it's there to help you- use as much or as little of it as you want.

Controller/Steam Deck play is kinda meh, but they're working on it over time. It's really meant to be a mouse/keyboard game.

Tl;dr, Wayward is chill vibes survival with very few bugs and good QOL, new features on the way, Steam Workshop support, and responsive devs. Give it a chance if you like the genre. :)

in its base settings Wayward is an unforgiving Roguelite that becomes easier with each playthrough as the crafting list fills out after each run.  It may take a few playthroughs before the mechanics begin to click, unless you've played similar games.  So allow me to share my insights regardless of your track with them.  As I am only about two-hundredish hours into what seems to be a much deeper experience than expected I appreciate your understanding.  

Cliffnotes-

To start-  Cut down a tree.  Press X to open dismantle menu (it is faster to use the dismantle menu than the mouse menu, especially with the aid of macros, although some important resources are next to otherwise dismantle only resources so be mindful.)  Dismantle all logs, sticks, and bark, in that order.  When sharpened items break, even if they don't, find a rock outcrop or a mountain tile and break it like the tree by "walking" into it.  Press C to open the crafting menu and find the stonecrafting menu, find sharp granite then craft it.  craft string from dismantled bark.  To organize inventory see bottom right of each individual inventory menu (each bag or chest outside inventory has its own organization.)  In C menu craft string, careful as the menu will suddenly expand with new options.  Once string is crafted make a spear, pick, and axe at the least.  Gather more bark and string to craft the bark armor in the woodworking menu.  Craft a granite or wood mortar and pestle and make tannin from bark, make skin from fur from a hunted bunny, make bone needle from dismantled bones, make string, convert skins to leather using tannin, make bags or backpacks, or waterskins, or leather clothes, snake skin makes outfit for hot biomes.  Gather 3 granite, 2 string, 4 poles, and 1 sharpened implement to craft a granite dripstone, craft at least 4 and place them next to the sea to keep them filled to stave off death.  This should be your first move in subsequent runs, unless playing rouseabout, as water is the hardest to manage unless you spawn near a mountain water source (finite) or underground water source (infinite,) which will need to be fire purified.  If you choose to explore first find apples ASAP as they will save you from thirst and hunger.  The higher your seafaring level, gained by boat travel in map, the less hunger, thirst, and item decay between island travel, level 100% likely no decomposition.  Dismantle 5 bark, and 2 sticks to make 2 torches to get through the first few nights, be sure to put out torches or place them on the ground if you intend to sleep unless you like waking up on fire (it sucks.)  To make a tier 2 bed gather 7 strings, and 2 poles, convert 4 strings into a rope and craft a hammock in the camping menu, unless you find a cotton plant skip tier 3 by keeping an eye out for feathers. Pay attention to tiers and thaumaturgical properties, i.e. purple hammocks are better than base feather bedrolls.  Gather granite to craft furnace and kiln, 16-48 granite (depending on luck,) plus chests and anvil.   Make a shovel, find gray tiles, harvest clay.  convert to bottle, gather bark, convert bark to corks, make fired bottles at kiln.  Glass follows similar path.  


The easiest house to build is a 4x4 cut into a mountain with a hallway door.  This allows for maximum expansion as you getr closer to 100% mining skill.  The fastest way to spawn a merchant is to raise your civilization level by adding self made floors, walls, doors, shelving, kiln & furnace, and a bed to the enclosed space.


Buttons to familiarize with-

O- letter not number- Gameplay Settings- controls settings such as; gather/drop, chop/harvest, mine/dig items, drop into containers, warn on destructive actions, warn of break on usage, use adjacent containers, etc.

V- Skills- Tracks skill % levels up to 100%.  Each skill is attached to a modifier, i.e. mining/leatherworking=strength (health/weight,) camping/tinkering=dexterity (stamina,) cooking/seafaring (metabolism/ hunger and thirst) 

U- Milestones- Keep track of your milestones that give gameplay modifiers as you discover more about the game such as; exsanguiniated- damage converts to bleed damage, Crafter- all crafts are 4x durability at a 1.3x more difficult, Diverse- all starting stats are decreased by 50% but gain at a +2 stat point per gain, etc.

U- Quests- Tutorial- Opens as the game is discovered.

Wayward is a true gem in the survival sandbox genre, offering an experience that’s both challenging and rewarding. It’s a game that truly captures the essence of adventure and exploration, keeping you hooked for hours as you strive to adapt and thrive in its procedurally generated world.

The game’s mechanics are impressively deep, yet accessible. You’ll find yourself scavenging for resources, crafting tools, and battling the elements—and sometimes creatures—all while managing your character’s health and stamina. The attention to detail is remarkable, with mechanics like item durability, realistic crafting, and even subtle interactions between objects that make the world feel alive and immersive.

What sets Wayward apart is its open-ended gameplay. There’s no hand-holding or fixed path; you make your own goals, and the game rewards experimentation and creativity. Whether you’re building a base, discovering new recipes, or mastering combat, every success feels earned, and every mistake teaches you something new.

The retro-style pixel art is charming, and the atmospheric soundtrack perfectly complements the game’s tone. Additionally, the developers at Unlok have done an outstanding job with community engagement, regularly updating the game based on player feedback and adding new features that keep the experience fresh.

I've had this game for years, but I never got into it because it just throws you in the deep end and the wiki wasn't super helpful for a long time. For some reason, though, it always called me back even though I would usually fumble around and die before I actually got anything done.
The past few days though, on probably my fifth try on learning this game, it all clicked and I started to understand what it's all about, and I've been loving every second of it! This is a roguelike survival game, essentially. I like that it is kind of open ended in playstyle. You can rush progress as fast as possible, or you can hang around on the starting island and be a stone-age caveman trying to survive, and both of those ways of playing are really fun! You can play as some kind of hunter-gatherer nomad who loves to explore or you can build a base and get whole setup to stockpile and prepare gear for a large expedition. The art style is charming and it has my favorite flavor of roguelike punishment, where anything that bad happens to you is a result of your own previous choices. There's never been a death where it felt like I was cheated. You die and learn lessons for your next character. Didn't bring enough or the proper gear for a new island and you die of dehydration? Remember to stock your boat with more water and food next time. Starved to death in your base because a strong predator set up camp right outside of your front door and you will 100% die if you fight it? Remember to build a secondary escape route next time. Your weapon broke in the middle of a right? remember to repair or reinforce your equipment before you need it next time.
I absolutely love this game so much and I think I'm going to stay addicted to it for a long time now. I totally recommend this diamond.
But again, the game does not hold your hand. Use the wiki, and use video tutorials for the beginning until you get the hang of it. Use items you don't need right now to craft items that you haven't before because new crafting recipes show up when you have the items needed to craft them. The game has so much more progression than it shows you at the start. For example, you don't get the recipe for a boat until you've made an oar and a rope, even though you don't have a reason to build an oar when you don't know where to get a boat. Honestly just build a chest and throw at least one of everything you find and can craft into it. It's confusing at first but the whole system starts to make sense when you get that hang of it, I promise!
Give this game a try for real <3
